runs.text: Long-run industry supply depends on input costs as firms enter or exit. In a constant-cost industry, expansion leaves input costs unchanged and long-run supply is horizontal. In an increasing-cost industry, expansion raises costs and supply slopes upward. In a decreasing-cost industry, expansion lowers costs and supply slopes downward.

runs.text: Price ($) is vertical; Industry quantity is horizontal. The long-run industry supply curve slopes upward. Industry expansion raises input costs, so sustaining a larger long-run quantity requires a higher price.

transcript.text: Price ($) is vertical; Industry quantity is horizontal. The long-run industry supply curve slopes upward. Industry expansion raises input costs, so sustaining a larger long-run quantity requires a higher price.

transcript.sourceText: The long-run industry supply curve slopes upward, rising from roughly $18 at very low output to above $50 near 105 units. Industry expansion therefore raises the long-run equilibrium price. That pattern is consistent with an increasing-cost industry in which entry bids up specialized inputs or other production costs.

THE CORE IDEA

Long-run industry supply depends on input costs as firms enter or exit. In a constant-cost industry, expansion leaves input costs unchanged and long-run supply is horizontal. In an increasing-cost industry, expansion raises costs and supply slopes upward. In a decreasing-cost industry, expansion lowers costs and supply slopes downward.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
Track input costs as the entire industry expands, not just one firm.
Unchanged, rising, or falling costs imply horizontal, upward, or downward long-run supply.
The displayed upward curve represents an increasing-cost industry.
WATCH OUT
Do not confuse industry cost conditions. If expansion does not change input costs, the long-run equilibrium price can return to the original cost level.

That pattern is consistent with an increasing-cost industry in which entry bids up specialized inputs or other production costs.
